name: Rickettsial Fever (Spotted Fever Group)

veryLikely: Rickettsia conorii / other spotted fever group Rickettsia species
possible: Orientia tsutsugamushi (if eschar is found on closer examination — would reclassify as scrub typhus)
pathogens.why: Spotted fever group rickettsioses are transmitted by ticks (rather than the chiggers/mites responsible for scrub typhus) and classically present with a generalized maculopapular or petechial rash rather than a single eschar, though clinical overlap exists and careful skin examination for an eschar should always be performed to distinguish from scrub typhus.

investigations.test: Careful skin examination for eschar and rash characterization
investigations.why: Helps distinguish spotted fever group rickettsiosis (maculopapular/petechial rash, no eschar) from scrub typhus (eschar), though management is similar.

investigations.test: Rickettsial serology (IgM/IgG, species-specific where available) or Weil-Felix (less specific)
investigations.why: Supports diagnosis, though treatment should not be delayed pending results when clinical suspicion is high.
Assesses organ involvement; thrombocytopenia and transaminitis are common supportive findings.

references: NCDC India Guidelines for Rickettsial Diseases
reason: Fever with maculopapular rash and headache, particularly with tick exposure history, is consistent with a spotted fever group rickettsial infection (distinct from scrub typhus, which classically presents with an eschar from chigger/mite bites rather than a generalized maculopapular rash from tick-borne transmission). Empiric doxycycline should be started promptly given the excellent and rapid response to treatment and the risk of progression if delayed.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.137-141 (Ch.21 Fever and Rash); p.1454-1459 (Ch.192 Rickettsial Diseases); p.1488 (Ch.189 Leptospirosis differential)
clinicalPearls: All acute rickettsial illnesses look alike for roughly the first 5 days: fever, headache, and myalgias, often with nausea, vomiting, or cough; the distinguishing features (rash, eschar, pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis) emerge only as the illness progresses (p.1454).

An inoculation eschar (tache noire) is a necrotic, often painless black-crusted lesion with a surrounding erythematous halo at the bite site; it can appear during the incubation period and is common in Mediterranean spotted fever (~50%), African tick-bite fever (~90%), and rickettsialpox (~90%), but is essentially absent in classic RMSF (<1%) and in epidemic/murine typhus (p.1455).

African tick-bite fever (R. africae) is the rickettsiosis most often imported into Europe and North America via travelers returning from sub-Saharan Africa; because Amblyomma ticks feed in groups, multiple eschars and regional lymphadenopathy are characteristic, and rash may be vesicular, sparse, or absent (p.1457-1458).

In RMSF the rash is centrifugal and evolving: erythematous macules begin on wrists and ankles, spread to extremities and trunk, and only later involve palms and soles; macules progress to non-blanching petechiae as vascular damage advances (p.1456).
Palm/sole involvement and the classic centripetal/centrifugal spread are late and inconsistent: in RMSF palms/soles are involved after day 5 in only ~43% and never in 18-64% of cases (p.1457).
The full classic triad of fever, rash, and recalled tick exposure is present in only ~3% of RMSF patients during the first 3 days, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1457).

Characteristic supportive labs across rickettsioses are thrombocytopenia, a normal or low (not elevated) WBC count, mildly elevated hepatic aminotransferases, and hyponatremia (p.1454-1456); hyponatremia in RMSF (~56%) reflects appropriate ADH secretion in a hypovolemic state (p.1457).
Spotted fever group serology cross-reacts among species, so a positive titer confirms a SFG rickettsiosis but generally cannot identify the specific organism (p.1458).
harrison.pathophysiology: Rickettsiae and Orientia are obligately intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli that primarily infect vascular endothelial cells. After tick saliva inoculates organisms into the dermis (in RMSF after roughly 6 h of feeding), they spread lymphohematogenously and infect contiguous foci of endothelium throughout the body, producing a widespread infectious vasculitis with increased vascular permeability. The resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia (rather than occlusive thrombosis) drive the organ injury: prerenal azotemia, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and CNS dysfunction. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in about a third to half of RMSF cases, but frank DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; the coagulation changes appear to be homeostatic responses to endothelial injury forming nonocclusive hemostatic plugs (p.1454, p.1456).
additionalDifferentials: Human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis (Ehrlichia chaffeensis) and human granulocytotropic anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) - tick-borne, often rashless, share thrombocytopenia/leukopenia/transaminitis (p.1455-1457)
Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus (R. prowazekii) and recrudescent Brill-Zinsser disease (p.1458)
infectionMimics: Influenza and enteroviral infection (mimic early rashless RMSF) (p.1457)
Leptospirosis (p.1457; shares epidemiologic and clinical features, dual infection reported, p.1488)
Typhoid fever (epidemic typhus is frequently misdiagnosed as typhoid in tropical countries) (p.1457-1458)
Gram-negative or gram-positive bacterial sepsis / septic shock (p.1457)
Dengue and hantavirus infection (share epidemiologic and clinical features) (p.1488)
additionalInvestigations: Indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) for SFG IgG - the most common confirmatory test; sensitivity 89-100% and specificity 99-100%, but a reactive titer (>=64) is not detectable until 7-10 days after onset and is usually negative at presentation (p.1458)
Immunohistologic examination or PCR of a 3-mm punch biopsy of a rash lesion - the only test useful during acute illness (immunohistology ~70% sensitive, 100% specific; PCR likely higher) (p.1458)
PCR of eschar biopsy or eschar swab, or skin biopsy, for SFG rickettsiae (p.1458)
Note: PCR of peripheral blood is NOT adequately sensitive because circulating organism quantities are low (p.1458)
Platelet count, WBC count, hepatic aminotransferases, serum sodium, and renal function as supportive clues (p.1454-1457)
CSF analysis if meningoencephalitis suspected (typically 10-100 cells/uL, mononuclear predominance, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein) (p.1456-1457)
redFlags: Hypotension/septic-shock presentation and multiorgan failure (p.1454, p.1457)
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS requiring mechanical ventilation (RMSF: ARDS ~12%) (p.1456-1457)
Encephalitis - confusion, lethargy, stupor, delirium, ataxia, seizures, or coma (p.1456-1457)
Acute kidney injury from acute tubular necrosis in shock (p.1457)
Skin necrosis, peripheral gangrene, or purpura fulminans (severe MSF) (p.1454; p.1488 / Ch.21)
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage; severe anemia requiring transfusion (p.1457)
Fulminant RMSF (fatal within 5 days), especially in male patients with G6PD deficiency (p.1457)
Extremes of age (children <10 years, adults >70 years) and immunosuppression - higher case-fatality (p.1456-1457)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome is strongly time-dependent: untreated RMSF carries mortality of roughly 20-25% (historic) with confirmed-case fatality around 9-10% where R. rickettsii is the sole agent, versus ~3-5% when treated early; delayed recognition and treatment markedly increase death. For unclear reasons RMSF case-fatality approaches 50% in Mexico and Brazil. Severe Mediterranean spotted fever has mortality near 50% without treatment but improves dramatically with even a single day of appropriate therapy. Untreated epidemic typhus historically killed up to 60% and still exceeds 10-15% in outbreaks. Many survivors of severe RMSF recover fully, but permanent neurologic deficits and gangrene requiring amputation can follow severe illness (p.1456-1457; p.1488 / Ch.21).
pitfalls: Waiting for serology before treating: SFG serology is typically negative at presentation and only turns positive at 7-10 days, so therapy must be started empirically on clinical and epidemiologic suspicion and never delayed for a confirmatory titer (p.1454, p.1458).

Excluding the diagnosis because there is no rash or no recalled tick bite: ~10-15% of RMSF patients never develop a rash, rash is present in only ~14% on day 1 and ~49% by day 3, and only ~60% recall a tick bite (p.1455-1457).

Treating a positive early SFG titer as proof of current disease: in areas with prevalent low-virulence SFG species (e.g., R. amblyommatis), a positive titer in the first 5-6 days often reflects preexisting cross-reactive antibody, not the acute illness (p.1456, p.1458).
Misattributing abdominal pain/vomiting to enterocolitis (has led to unnecessary laparotomy) or CNS findings to primary meningoencephalitis (p.1457).
Using ineffective or harmful agents: beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, and erythromycin have no role in RMSF, and sulfa drugs are associated with worse outcomes than no treatment (p.1458).

Missing the eschar: it can be small, painless, and located in skinfolds/scalp and frequently goes unnoticed by patient and clinician, yet careful skin examination for an eschar is a key diagnostic clue (p.1454-1459).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal grading scale, but stratifies along a spectrum: (1) self-limited febrile illness that resolves without evolution; (2) classic disease with rash and/or eschar; and (3) severe/complicated disease with organ involvement - pneumonitis/ARDS, meningoencephalitis, acute kidney injury, hemorrhage/skin necrosis/gangrene, sepsis/septic shock, and (rarely) fulminant RMSF fatal within 5 days. Higher-risk groups include children <10 years, adults >70 years, the immunosuppressed, and (for fulminant RMSF) males with G6PD deficiency (p.1454-1457).
